Feature Specification ID: SPEC-17
Title: Antivirus Exclusion Script Deployment for Remote Management Tool — POS Terminal Validation
Change Type: Security / infrastructure (script deployment and antivirus configuration)
System Area: POS terminals, Windows Defender antivirus, remote management tooling

Description:
A new remote management script has been created that adds Windows Defender antivirus exclusions for the latest version of a remote tunneling tool used for store support access. POS terminals at some store locations have recently flagged this tool as a potential security threat, preventing remote support sessions. The script must be tested across multiple lab environments. After the script is executed, QA must verify that the POS terminals continue to function normally, that the remote management tool is no longer flagged, and that no unexpected system behaviour results from the exclusion being applied.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

clarification_flags: Are there multiple POS terminal hardware models or tablet models that each require individual certificate import validation?
Is mutual TLS (client certificate authentication) in use, or is this a one-way server certificate only?
What is the exact mechanism for the certificate import process — is it a script, agent, MDM push, or manual process — and can it be triggered on demand in UAT?
How many content management page settings reference the certificate, and will all of them be updated as part of this change?
Has the external loyalty platform vendor confirmed installation of the new certificate on their servers, and is there a test endpoint available for validation?
What happens to in-flight loyalty transactions during the certificate cutover — is there a maintenance window or is this expected to be seamless?
Are there any certificate pinning implementations in the POS or tablet applications that would require an application update alongside the certificate rotation?
What is the rollback plan if the new certificate causes issues after deployment, and has it been tested?
Will POS terminals and tablets that are offline during the deployment window receive the new certificate automatically when they reconnect, and by what deadline?
Is the new UAT environment zone a full replica of the production configuration, or are there known differences that could affect test validity?

coverage_depth.justification: SSL certificate rotation is a security-critical infrastructure change with a hard deadline tied to certificate expiry. Failure would cause complete service disruption for loyalty platform integration across all affected POS terminals and tablets for the impacted brand. The multi-device, multi-layer nature (POS, tablets, CMS config, external vendor) increases risk surface and warrants thorough coverage.

effort_estimate.notes: Estimate accounts for device-type variations (POS terminals vs. tablets), UAT environment zone validation, and the need to test both the import process and the downstream integration behavior. Effort may increase if multiple POS terminal models or tablet configurations require individual validation, or if the number of content management page settings is large. Coordination with the external loyalty vendor for integration test windows should be factored into scheduling.

exploratory_tests: Explore POS terminal and tablet behavior when the old (expiring) certificate is presented instead of the new one — confirm rejection or graceful error
Explore what happens if the certificate import process fails mid-way on a device — assess recovery and retry behavior
Explore edge cases where content management page settings reference a missing or misconfigured certificate zone
Explore behavior on POS terminals or tablets that may have been offline during the certificate import window
Explore whether any hardcoded certificate references or pinned certificates exist in the POS or tablet applications that could cause failures

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-18
Title: POS Crew Notification Feature Enablement on POS Workstations
Change Type: New feature (POS notification scheduling and display system)
System Area: POS workstation, employee clock-in workflow, notification management

Description:
A POS notification feature is being enabled on POS workstations. This feature allows store owners and managers to schedule messages that will appear on POS workstation screens when a crew member clocks in. Notifications can be used to communicate information such as new promotional offers, loyalty program reminders, upsell prompts during checkout, or changes in store policy and procedures. The feature is intended to help owners and managers communicate with staff even when they are not physically present at the store.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-01
Title: Online Ordering Portal Still Shows Menu Item as Available After Overnight Menu Sync
Change Type: Bug fix / Integration patch
System Area: POS to online ordering platform integration (menu sync)

Description:
When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

Acceptance Criteria:
- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-13
Title: POS Hierarchy Zone Addition for Full-Menu Non-Traditional Store Locations
Change Type: Configuration change (new zone addition to hierarchy)
System Area: POS configuration, hierarchy and zone management, menu and page design

Description:
A new zone is being added to the non-traditional store network and properties hierarchy to support retail locations that carry the full brand menu. The new zone is designed to inherit the standard brand POS configuration rather than the limited-menu page design used by other non-traditional locations. Specifically, the new zone should pull down standard brand configuration and the correct full-menu page design, excluding the limited-menu bakery and beverage-only page design used at other non-traditional sites. Testing should confirm that the correct configuration and page design are pulled down for properties assigned to the new zone.

Title: Digital Ordering App Version Upgrade — Multi-Device and Multi-OS Compatibility Testing
Change Type: Version upgrade (third-party application)
System Area: Tablet-based digital ordering application, device and OS compatibility

Description:
A new version of the digital ordering application has been released by the third-party vendor and is ready for QA testing. You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

Title: POS Hierarchy Zone Addition for Full-Menu Non-Traditional Store Locations
Change Type: Configuration change (new zone addition to hierarchy)
System Area: POS configuration, hierarchy and zone management, menu and page design

Testing should confirm that the correct configuration and page design are pulled down for properties assigned to the new zone.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

Title: Role-Based Access Control — Restrict Void on Empty Check for Fraud Prevention
Change Type: Security / access control configuration change
System Area: POS role configuration, transaction management

Description:
A fraud pattern has been identified where external actors instruct store staff to initiate a void on an empty check, bypassing the standard transaction return process. A system option bit exists to block this behavior at the role level. This option bit will be disabled for all roles that currently have it enabled, across both brands. Roles with no change (already require authorization): Brand A — Crew, Crew Plus; Brand B — Crew Member, Senior Crew Member. Testing should confirm the restriction blocks the fraud pattern without disrupting legitimate operations such as voiding individual items, transaction returns, and opening closed checks. Note: the scenario is replicable using a food item order, not a beverage order.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

You are a senior software quality assurance analyst. Given a software feature specification, produce an actionable manual test scope recommendation.

Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.
2. Identify adjacent core workflows that need a quick confidence check.
3. Identify existing behavior that could regress because of the change.
4. Identify integrations, interfaces, and end-to-end data flows that may be affected.
5. Identify boundary conditions, failure paths, timing issues, and other useful exploratory scenarios.
6. Assign LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH coverage depth by considering user and business impact, regression surface, integration criticality, reversibility, and uncertainty.
7. Estimate a realistic range of manual test cases for a small QA team.
8. Identify specific missing information that could change the recommended scope.

Base the recommendation only on the supplied specification. Do not invent system behavior or dependencies. Make each test description concrete enough for a QA practitioner to act on.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).

You are a senior software quality assurance analyst. Given a software feature specification, produce an actionable manual test scope recommendation.

Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.
2. Identify adjacent core workflows that need a quick confidence check.
3. Identify existing behavior that could regress because of the change.
4. Identify integrations, interfaces, and end-to-end data flows that may be affected.
5. Identify boundary conditions, failure paths, timing issues, and other useful exploratory scenarios.

7. Estimate a realistic range of manual test cases for a small QA team.

Base the recommendation only on the supplied specification. Do not invent system behavior or dependencies. Make each test description concrete enough for a QA practitioner to act on.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-01
Title: Online Ordering Portal Still Shows Menu Item as Available After Overnight Menu Sync
Change Type: Bug fix / Integration patch
System Area: POS to online ordering platform integration (menu sync)

Description:
When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

Acceptance Criteria:
- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

You are a senior software quality assurance analyst. Given a software feature specification, produce an actionable manual test scope recommendation.

Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.
2. Identify adjacent core workflows that need a quick confidence check.
3. Identify existing behavior that could regress because of the change.
4. Identify integrations, interfaces, and end-to-end data flows that may be affected.
5. Identify boundary conditions, failure paths, timing issues, and other useful exploratory scenarios.

7. Estimate a realistic range of manual test cases for a small QA team.
8. Identify specific missing information that could change the recommended scope.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-01
Title: Online Ordering Portal Still Shows Menu Item as Available After Overnight Menu Sync
Change Type: Bug fix / Integration patch
System Area: POS to online ordering platform integration (menu sync)

Description:
When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

Acceptance Criteria:
- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

Because DNS resolution underpins all network-dependent system functions, this change has broad potential impact and requires regression testing across all major integrated areas. Areas to be tested include but are not limited to: payment device connectivity, Wi-Fi network connectivity, remote management tool functions, kitchen display system order routing, order storing and picking, digital menu board and price change functionality, delivery platform integrations, online ordering platform orders, gift card and loyalty processing in offline mode, database reload and refresh, reporting and analytics, employee creation workflows, sales performance notification tools, and third-party order alert integrations.

    "Confirm that database reload and refresh operations complete successfully when DNS resolution is handled by the secondary provider",
    "Verify that reporting and analytics data pipelines resolve their target endpoints correctly via secondary DNS",
    "Confirm that employee creation workflows that depend on network-authenticated directory or identity services succeed under secondary DNS",
    "Verify that sales performance notification tools (e.g., email or push alert services) resolve their delivery endpoints via secondary DNS",

    "Confirm that gift card and loyalty processing in offline mode (no DNS resolution available) continues to function as per existing offline fallback logic",
    "Verify that order storing and picking workflows complete without errors under normal dual-DNS conditions",
    "Confirm that scheduled database reload and refresh jobs execute on their normal cadence without DNS-related timeouts",
    "Verify that all standard reports (sales summary, labour, inventory) generate correctly and contain accurate data after the DNS change",
    "Confirm that employee creation and role assignment workflows complete without errors in the identity/directory system",
    "Verify that price change propagation from back-office to digital menu boards follows the existing schedule and accuracy",
    "Confirm that third-party order alert integrations continue to fire alerts within SLA thresholds under normal DNS conditions",
    "Verify that the remote management tool's scheduled tasks (e.g., software pushes, config deployments) execute without DNS resolution failures",
    "Confirm that sales performance notifications are delivered to the correct recipients on the expected schedule after the DNS change"

    "Simulate primary DNS failure and verify that payment processor hostname resolution automatically falls over to Google Public DNS without transaction failure or unacceptable latency increase",

    "Simulate primary DNS failure and verify that the KDS order routing service resolves its upstream endpoints via secondary DNS without order loss or duplication",
    "Simulate primary DNS failure and verify that reporting data pipeline connections to analytics endpoints resolve via secondary DNS and data is not dropped",
    "Simulate primary DNS failure and verify that the remote management tool maintains device connectivity via secondary DNS",
    "Simulate primary DNS failure and verify that third-party order alert integrations (webhook or API-based) continue to deliver alerts via secondary DNS",
    "Verify that DNS TTL expiry and cache refresh behaviour is consistent between the old secondary provider and Google Public DNS for all critical hostnames",
    "Verify that any TLS/SSL certificate validation for payment and integration endpoints is not adversely affected by the change in DNS resolver (e.g., no DNSSEC or resolver-policy conflicts)",

  "exploratory_tests": [
    "Probe DNS resolution response time differences between the old secondary provider and Google Public DNS for all critical hostnames, and assess whether any latency increase causes transaction timeouts or UI degradation",
    "Investigate whether any integrated system has hardcoded DNS server addresses or resolver configurations that would prevent it from using the new secondary DNS",
    "Explore behaviour when both primary and secondary DNS are simultaneously unavailable — confirm that offline fallback modes (e.g., loyalty, gift card) activate correctly and do not attempt indefinite DNS retries that degrade POS performance",
    "Probe whether Google Public DNS returns different IP addresses (e.g., due to GeoDNS or anycast differences) for payment processor or CDN hostnames compared to the previous secondary provider, and assess whether those IPs are whitelisted in firewall rules",
    "Investigate whether any system component enforces DNSSEC validation and whether Google Public DNS DNSSEC behaviour is compatible with those components",

clarification_flags: Where exactly is the locked price stored — in the mobile app order payload, the order management database, or both — and which system is the authoritative source when the POS processes the order at fulfillment?

Does the POS re-query the pricing engine at fulfillment time, or does it consume the price values embedded in the order record? This is critical to understanding whether a price lock is architecturally enforced or assumed.

What is the payment model — is the customer charged in full at time of ordering, or is a hold placed and the final charge occurs at fulfillment? This affects which price-lock scenarios are financially relevant.
Is there any existing price-lock or order-snapshot mechanism documented in the system design, or is this behavior assumed/untested?
What admin interface or API is used to change item prices, and how quickly do price changes propagate to the systems involved (real-time, batch, cached)?
Are there any known environments or test data sets where advance orders and price changes can be safely simulated without affecting production data?
Does the scope include testing on both iOS and Android mobile app clients, and are there any known platform-specific differences in how orders are submitted?
Are promotions, coupons, or loyalty discounts applied at order time also expected to be locked, or only the base item price?
What constitutes a 'price change' in this system — only manual admin updates, or also automated pricing rules, surge pricing, or scheduled price changes?

coverage_depth.justification: This scenario has explicit product-decision urgency, involves financial data integrity (customers are charged real money at locked prices), spans multiple integrated systems (mobile app, pricing engine, order management, POS, payment processor), and the expected behavior has not been confirmed — meaning the outcome is unknown and regression risk is high. Thorough coverage is required to produce a reliable finding.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes a single test environment with stable pricing engine access and direct POS inspection capability. Upper bound accounts for testing across multiple item types, price change magnitudes, and any additional edge cases surfaced during exploratory sessions. A small team of 2 QA practitioners should plan for 3–5 days including environment setup, test execution, and findings documentation given the cross-system nature of the flows.

exploratory_tests: Explore what happens when an item in an advance order is marked as a different price tier or category (not just a price value change) before fulfillment — does the POS still honor the locked price?
Explore behavior when an item in an advance order is discontinued or removed from the menu entirely before the pickup time — does the order error, process at the old price, or drop the item?

Explore what happens if a price change is made and then reverted to the original price before fulfillment — does the system process correctly and are there any duplicate-charge or reconciliation anomalies?

Explore the scenario where the advance order pickup time window is missed by the customer and the order is fulfilled late (e.g., several hours after scheduled time) during which a price change occurred — does the lock still hold?
Explore whether the locked price is preserved if the customer modifies the advance order (e.g., changes quantity) after placement but before fulfillment, and a price change has also occurred.

Explore edge cases around tax calculation: if the item price is locked but tax rates change before fulfillment, does the system apply the original or new tax rate, and is the total consistent with what was charged?
Explore concurrent scenarios: simulate multiple advance orders for the same item being fulfilled simultaneously after a price change to check for race conditions or inconsistent price application.
Explore what error messages or behaviors surface on the POS if there is any price mismatch detected at fulfillment — are staff given actionable information or does the order silently fail?
functional_tests: Place an advance order for a single item via the mobile app, complete payment, then change that item's price in the system before the scheduled pickup time; verify the POS receives and processes the order at the original locked price.

Place an advance order for multiple items via the mobile app, complete payment, then change the price of every ordered item before fulfillment; verify each item on the POS order reflects the price at time of ordering, not the updated price.

Place an advance order for multiple items, change the price of only a subset of items before fulfillment; verify that changed-price items retain the locked price and unchanged-price items also reflect the correct original price.
Place an advance order and increase an item's price before fulfillment; verify the customer is not charged the higher price and the POS order total matches the original payment amount.
Place an advance order and decrease an item's price before fulfillment; verify the customer is not automatically refunded the difference and the POS order total matches the original payment amount.
Verify the order confirmation displayed in the mobile app after payment shows the locked prices and total that were charged.
Verify the order detail screen in the mobile app on the day of pickup (before fulfillment) still displays the original locked prices, not the updated prices.
Verify the receipt or order summary presented at POS fulfillment shows the locked prices and matches the amount already collected from the customer.

Place an advance order, change an item's price multiple times between order placement and fulfillment; verify the POS processes the order at the price that was active at the moment of payment, not any intermediate or final price.
Place an advance order for an item, change its price to zero (free) before fulfillment; verify the POS does not process the item as free and retains the locked price.
integration_tests: Verify the payload sent from the mobile app to the POS at fulfillment time contains the price-locked line item amounts and that the POS does not re-query the pricing engine to recalculate item prices at fulfillment.
Verify the payment processor transaction amount matches the POS order total at fulfillment when a price change has occurred between order placement and pickup.
Simulate a pricing engine update via the admin/back-office interface and confirm the change propagates correctly to new orders while advance orders in the queue remain unaffected.
Verify that if the POS system is restarted or reconnected between order placement and fulfillment, the advance order still retains the locked price when it is loaded.
Verify the data stored in the order management system for an advance order records the locked price at time of payment, and that this stored value is what is transmitted to the POS at fulfillment.

Test the end-to-end flow across mobile app, order management system, pricing engine, and POS to confirm no system in the chain silently overwrites the locked price with the current price during order transmission or processing.
regression_tests: Place and fulfill a same-day immediate order (non-advance) after a price change has been made; verify the immediate order correctly uses the current updated price, confirming price changes still apply to non-locked orders.

Place an advance order, do not change any prices, and fulfill it at the scheduled time; verify the order processes correctly end-to-end with no errors, confirming the advance order flow itself has not regressed.
Verify that a price change made in the pricing engine is correctly reflected for new orders placed after the change, confirming the pricing engine update mechanism still functions.
Verify that canceling an advance order after a price change has occurred still triggers the correct refund at the original charged amount.
Verify that loyalty points, discounts, or promotions applied at time of advance order placement are preserved through fulfillment regardless of price changes.
Verify that the order history in the customer's mobile app account shows the correct locked price paid, not the current item price.
smoke_tests: Place a basic advance order for one item via the mobile app with a next-day pickup time and confirm payment completes successfully at the displayed price.
Verify the advance order appears in the POS queue at the scheduled pickup time.
Verify the POS can open and process a standard advance order without a price change having occurred, confirming the baseline fulfillment flow is intact.

You are a senior software quality assurance analyst. Given a software feature specification, produce an actionable manual test scope recommendation.

Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.
2. Identify adjacent core workflows that need a quick confidence check.
3. Identify existing behavior that could regress because of the change.
4. Identify integrations, interfaces, and end-to-end data flows that may be affected.
5. Identify boundary conditions, failure paths, timing issues, and other useful exploratory scenarios.
6. Assign LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH coverage depth by considering user and business impact, regression surface, integration criticality, reversibility, and uncertainty.
7. Estimate a realistic range of manual test cases for a small QA team.
8. Identify specific missing information that could change the recommended scope.

Base the recommendation only on the supplied specification. Do not invent system behavior or dependencies. Make each test description concrete enough for a QA practitioner to act on.

Return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences or any text outside the JSON object.

JSON schema:
{
  "spec_id": "string",
  "functional_tests": ["test description"],
  "smoke_tests": ["test description"],
  "regression_tests": ["test description"],
  "integration_tests": ["test description"],
  "exploratory_tests": ["test description"],
  "coverage_depth": {
    "level": "LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH",
    "justification": "brief reason"
  },
  "effort_estimate": {
    "min_test_cases": 0,
    "max_test_cases": 0,
    "notes": "brief notes"
  },
  "clarification_flags": ["missing information that would affect testing"]
}

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-11
Title: Mobile App Advance Order — Price Lock Behavior When Item Prices Change Before Fulfillment
Change Type: Exploratory / edge case validation
System Area: Mobile ordering app, pricing engine, POS order processing

Description:
A customer places an advance order for multiple items via the mobile app, selects a future pickup time (e.g., next day 9:00 AM), and completes payment at the current price. Before the order is fulfilled, the price of one or more ordered items is changed in the system. The expected behavior is that the order processes at the price locked in at the time of ordering, with no errors or price discrepancies when the mobile app sends the order to the POS the following day. The objective is to confirm or disprove this expected behavior. This scenario has urgency as a product decision depends on the outcome.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-01
Title: Online Ordering Portal Still Shows Menu Item as Available After Overnight Menu Sync
Change Type: Bug fix / Integration patch
System Area: POS to online ordering platform integration (menu sync)

Description:
When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

Acceptance Criteria:
- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-01
Title: Online Ordering Portal Still Shows Menu Item as Available After Overnight Menu Sync
Change Type: Bug fix / Integration patch
System Area: POS to online ordering platform integration (menu sync)

Description:
When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

Acceptance Criteria:
- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

Title: Menu Item Availability App — Time Window Configuration Enhancement
Change Type: Enhancement (software behavior change in version update)
System Area: POS extension app / menu item scheduling

Description:
A new build of the Menu Item Availability extension app changes how scheduling windows are configured. Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.

Base the recommendation only on the supplied specification. Do not invent system behavior or dependencies. Make each test description concrete enough for a QA practitioner to act on.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

{

  "functional_tests": ["test description"],

clarification_flags: How many distinct POS terminal models and tablet models are in scope — are there hardware or OS differences that would require the certificate import process to be tested on each variant separately?
Is the certificate import process automated (e.g. pushed via MDM or a platform script) or manually executed on each device — this materially affects both test approach and deployment risk?

Does the UAT environment zone fully replicate the production loyalty platform integration, or is it a stub/mock — if the vendor has only installed the new certificate in production, UAT testing of the SSL handshake may not be valid?

What is the rollout strategy — simultaneous update of all devices or phased? If phased, is there a period where some devices carry the old certificate while the vendor's server has already switched, and how is this handled?
Are there multiple content management page settings or configuration entries that reference the certificate, or a single entry? If multiple, all must be identified and updated.
Is the affected brand the only tenant on this loyalty platform integration, or do other brands share the same integration endpoint with separate certificates — confirming blast radius of the change?
What is the process for verifying successful certificate import across the full device estate in production — is there a reporting or audit mechanism, or must each device be checked individually?

Has the external loyalty platform vendor confirmed installation of the new certificate on their servers in the UAT environment zone, and is there a point of contact for coordinating SSL handshake validation during testing?

Are there any network intermediaries (load balancers, reverse proxies, API gateways) between the POS/tablet and the loyalty platform that perform SSL termination and would also require certificate updates?
What is the rollback plan if the new certificate causes integration failures post-deployment — is reverting to the old certificate possible given its imminent expiry?

coverage_depth.justification: Certificate rotation is a LOW change type by classification. However, the involvement of external vendor coordination, multiple device types, a content management configuration dependency, and a hard expiry deadline introduce moderate operational risk. Coverage is therefore thorough for a LOW change but does not extend to full feature regression across the broader platform.

effort_estimate.notes: Estimate assumes one QA tester executing manually in the UAT environment zone across one POS terminal and one tablet as representative devices. If multiple device models or OS versions are in scope, add approximately 5–8 cases per additional device variant. Vendor-side certificate verification may require coordination time not reflected in case count.

Explore the experience on a device that has not yet received the new certificate attempting to connect to the loyalty platform after the vendor has already switched to the new certificate on their server

messages.content:
You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change

- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-01
Title: Online Ordering Portal Still Shows Menu Item as Available After Overnight Menu Sync
Change Type: Bug fix / Integration patch
System Area: POS to online ordering platform integration (menu sync)

Description:
When a menu item is marked as Out of Stock on the POS, the system is expected to propagate this status to the online ordering portal after the configured sync interval. However, even after leaving the system overnight to complete a full menu sync cycle, the item continues to appear as available in the online portal. Customers who attempt to add the item to their cart receive an error message at checkout rather than seeing the item correctly flagged as unavailable.

Acceptance Criteria:
- The item should display Out of Stock status on the POS immediately after being marked as such.
- The item should not be orderable on the online web and mobile ordering apps after being marked out of stock.
- After the Out of Stock flag is removed and saved, the item should become visible and orderable again on both POS and online ordering apps.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:

    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

JSON schema:
{
  "spec_id": "string",
  "functional_tests": ["test description"],
  "smoke_tests": ["test description"],
  "regression_tests": ["test description"],
  "integration_tests": ["test description"],
  "exploratory_tests": ["test description"],
  "coverage_depth": {
    "level": "LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH",
    "justification": "brief reason"
  },
  "effort_estimate": {
    "min_test_cases": 0,
    "max_test_cases": 0,
    "notes": "brief notes"
  },
  "clarification_flags": ["missing information that would affect testing"]
}

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-12
Title: Financial Report Layout Change — Move Third-Party Delivery Detail Section to Bottom
Change Type: Enhancement (report layout / section reordering)
System Area: Financial reporting (property-level report)

Description:
On the Property Financial Report, the Third-Party Delivery Partner detailed sales data section currently prints under the Order Type section, where it provides supporting detail for the sales summarized in that section. Franchisees and accountants have requested this detailed section be relocated to the bottom of the report, below the Rewards section. The intent is to elevate the visibility of Tender Media, Group Sales, Discounts, and Service Charges sections, which currently appear after the delivery detail block. The summary-level delivery sales in the Order Type section should remain unchanged and continue to display correctly.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

clarification_flags: Is 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION' a valid message for any other transaction type or scenario on this terminal? If so, those scenarios must be explicitly protected in regression testing.

What is the exact mechanism for disabling backend cloud processing — is it a terminal setting, a network configuration, or a backend toggle — and does this state need to be verified before each test run?
Are there multiple POS terminal models or firmware versions in scope, and does the configuration fix need to be validated independently on each?
What is the deployment mechanism for the corrected configuration files (e.g., pushed remotely, loaded at startup, manually applied), and could a re-deployment revert the fix?
Is there a specific configuration file name or key/value pair that was changed, so testers can directly inspect and verify the fix at the file level?
Does the cancel action trigger any backend event, receipt, or audit log entry that also needs to reflect the corrected cancel type?
Are there any other terminal messages that share the same configuration key or template as the incorrect message, which could also be affected by the fix?
What POS software version will be used during validation, and is this fix isolated to a specific version or applied broadly?

coverage_depth.justification: Although this is a targeted bug fix to a display message, the root cause involves mismatched configuration files which carry a broad regression risk across multiple message types and transaction flows. The fix must be validated specifically with cloud processing disabled as specified, and any misconfiguration could silently affect other terminal messages or transaction states. The financial nature of gift card processing and the crew-facing impact of incorrect messaging elevate business and operational risk, warranting thorough coverage.

effort_estimate.notes: The lower bound covers the core functional, smoke, and critical regression scenarios. The upper bound accounts for testing across multiple terminal hardware variants, additional gift card transaction stages, and exploratory edge cases. Effort scales significantly if multiple POS terminal models or software versions require independent validation.

exploratory_tests: Toggle backend cloud processing on and off rapidly, then cancel a gift card transaction, and observe whether the terminal displays the correct message or reverts to the incorrect one.
Attempt to cancel a gift card transaction when the gift card has a zero balance and observe the terminal message displayed.
Simulate a network interruption (separate from cloud processing toggle) during a gift card cancel and observe whether the correct 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' message still appears.
Check whether the incorrect 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION' message can still be triggered on the terminal through any other transaction flow or button sequence after the fix is applied.
Observe terminal behavior if the crew member cancels a gift card transaction immediately after card presentation (before any amount is entered) and confirm the correct message displays.
Review the configuration files directly to confirm the override or mismatched entry has been removed or corrected, and that no duplicate or conflicting keys exist for the cancel message string.

Test cancel behavior on a gift card transaction that spans a split-tender scenario (gift card plus another payment method) with cloud processing disabled, and verify the displayed message is appropriate.
functional_tests: With backend cloud processing disabled, initiate a gift card transaction on the POS terminal and cancel it mid-transaction; verify the terminal displays exactly 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' and not 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION'.
With backend cloud processing disabled, verify that the 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' message appears within an acceptable time after the crew member triggers the cancel action on a gift card transaction.

With backend cloud processing disabled, cancel a gift card transaction at different stages (e.g., after card swipe/tap, after amount entry, before final confirmation) and confirm 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' is displayed at each stage.
Confirm that after the 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' message is displayed, the POS terminal returns to its idle or ready state without error.
Verify that no residual 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION' message text appears anywhere on the terminal screen during or after a gift card cancel action with cloud processing disabled.
Confirm the corrected configuration files are deployed to the terminal and that no override configuration is re-applying the old incorrect message string.
Verify that cancelling a gift card transaction with cloud processing disabled does not leave the gift card balance in an inconsistent or partially debited state.
integration_tests: With backend cloud processing disabled, cancel a gift card transaction and verify the cancellation event is correctly logged in any local transaction or audit log, referencing the correct cancel action type.
With backend cloud processing re-enabled after testing, cancel a gift card transaction and confirm the terminal-to-backend communication correctly reflects a cancel event with no message mismatch.
Verify that the configuration file correction is consistently applied across all POS terminal models or hardware variants in use, not just the terminal used during initial validation.
Confirm that the corrected configuration files do not conflict with any other active configuration or override files loaded at terminal startup or during transaction processing.
If a receipt is generated upon gift card transaction cancel, verify the receipt text reflects the correct cancel action and does not reference 'VOID NEW ITEMS'.
regression_tests: With backend cloud processing enabled, cancel a gift card transaction and verify the correct cancel message is displayed, confirming the fix does not break cloud-enabled behavior.

Perform a standard non-gift-card transaction cancel (e.g., cash or credit card) and verify the correct message for that transaction type still displays, confirming no cross-contamination from the configuration fix.

Verify that the 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION' message still appears correctly in any scenario where it is legitimately expected (e.g., voiding new items on a non-gift-card transaction), confirming the message was not globally removed.
Complete a full gift card transaction (no cancel) with cloud processing disabled and confirm the success/completion message is unaffected by the configuration change.
Complete a full gift card transaction (no cancel) with cloud processing enabled and confirm the success/completion message is unaffected.
Verify that other POS terminal display messages (e.g., insufficient balance, invalid card, transaction approved) are unchanged after the configuration file correction.
Cancel a gift card transaction multiple times in succession with cloud processing disabled and confirm consistent display of 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' each time without message drift or caching issues.
smoke_tests: With backend cloud processing disabled, cancel a single gift card transaction and confirm the terminal displays 'CANCEL TRANSACTION'.
Confirm the POS terminal successfully loads and operates in a state where backend cloud processing is turned off before beginning gift card cancel testing.
Initiate and complete (not cancel) a gift card transaction with cloud processing disabled to confirm baseline gift card processing still functions.

Use a general risk-based QA planning process:
1. Identify the behavior directly changed and the expected outcomes to verify.
2. Identify adjacent core workflows that need a quick confidence check.
3. Identify existing behavior that could regress because of the change.
4. Identify integrations, interfaces, and end-to-end data flows that may be affected.
5. Identify boundary conditions, failure paths, timing issues, and other useful exploratory scenarios.
6. Assign LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH coverage depth by considering user and business impact, regression surface, integration criticality, reversibility, and uncertainty.
7. Estimate a realistic range of manual test cases for a small QA team.
8. Identify specific missing information that could change the recommended scope.

Base the recommendation only on the supplied specification. Do not invent system behavior or dependencies. Make each test description concrete enough for a QA practitioner to act on.

Return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences or any text outside the JSON object.

Feature Specification ID: SPEC-15
Title: Gift Card Transaction Cancel Messaging Fix — Validate Correct Terminal Display With Cloud Processing Disabled
Change Type: Bug fix (UI messaging mismatch caused by mismatched configuration files)
System Area: Gift card processing, POS terminal display, backend cloud processing

Description:
Mismatched configuration files are causing the wrong message to display on the POS terminal when a crew member cancels a gift card transaction. The correct expected message is CANCEL TRANSACTION. However, the terminal is currently displaying VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION, which is incorrect for this action. The root cause is either an override that needs to be removed or configuration files that need to be corrected. Validation should be performed with backend cloud processing turned off to confirm the correct message displays.

Provide your test scope recommendation as a JSON object matching the schema.

clarification_flags: Is the markup change prospective only (applying to transactions on/after the effective date) or retroactive (recalculating all historical transactions for the targeted platform)? This fundamentally changes the regression and integration test scope.

Are both brands configured independently in the Data Mapping settings, or do they share a common configuration that is toggled per brand? This affects whether a change to one brand could inadvertently affect the other.
Which specific third-party delivery platform is affected? Knowing the platform name is needed to scope integration tests and identify the correct data pipeline path.

What is the mechanism for the effective date enforcement — is it a date field in the configuration tool, a manual deployment step, or a scheduled pipeline job? This affects how the cutover boundary is tested.

Is Production testing limited to read-only verification of the configuration value and live report outputs, or is a configuration change also being applied in Production as part of this QA cycle?

coverage_depth.justification: Although this is a configuration value change (typically LOW risk), the multi-environment requirement (UAT, Pre-Prod, Production), the involvement of a data pipeline, a separate third-party reporting platform, two brands, and the unresolved retroactivity question elevate the risk and scope to MEDIUM. Incorrect markup values directly affect financial reporting and contractual compliance, increasing the consequence of any defect.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes retroactivity question is resolved before testing begins, the third-party reporting platform change is out of scope or handled separately, and environments are stable. Upper bound accounts for testing across all three environments (UAT, Pre-Prod, Production), both brands tested independently, retroactive and prospective scenarios both requiring coverage, and exploratory sessions adding unscripted cases. Explore whether the change to one brand's Data Mapping setting could inadvertently affect the other brand's configuration if they share a common config layer or template
Probe historical report views: run a report spanning both before and after the effective date and verify that the markup split is correctly represented and not uniformly overwritten
Investigate audit trail completeness — confirm that the configuration change is logged with the previous value (25%), new value (26%), effective date, and the identity of the user who made the change

Explore the scenario where the third-party reporting platform has not yet applied their corresponding change — verify what discrepancy this produces and whether it is detectable in reconciliation reports

functional_tests: Verify that the delivery markup percentage for the targeted third-party delivery platform is updated from 25% to 26% in the Data Mapping settings of the reporting/analytics configuration tool
Verify that the markup change applies to both Brand A and Brand B transactions for the targeted delivery platform, and confirm each brand independently

Verify that saving the Data Mapping configuration change produces a confirmation state (success message, audit log entry, or equivalent) and does not silently fail

Verify that the data pipeline continues to ingest and process transaction records from the targeted delivery platform without errors or dropped records after the configuration change

Verify that the data pipeline does not re-process or duplicate historical transactions as a side-effect of the configuration update
smoke_tests: Confirm the reporting/analytics configuration tool is accessible and the Data Mapping settings section loads without error in UAT, Pre-Production, and Production
Confirm that at least one post-effective-date transaction for the targeted delivery platform appears in reports with the 26% markup applied
Confirm that at least one transaction for a different (unaffected) delivery platform shows no change to its markup value in reports
Confirm that both brands can be queried in the reporting tool and return results without errors after the configuration change

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:

You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

{
  "spec_id": "string",
  "functional_tests": ["test description"],
  "smoke_tests": ["test description"],
  "regression_tests": ["test description"],
  "integration_tests": ["test description"],
  "exploratory_tests": ["test description"],

The objective is to confirm or disprove this expected behavior. This scenario has urgency as a product decision depends on the outcome.

Change Type: Enhancement (software behavior change in version update)

messages.content:
You are ATSR (AI-assisted Test Scope Recommender), an expert QA analyst specialising in manual testing for enterprise software systems, including point-of-sale, reporting, and integration-heavy platforms.

Your role is to analyse a feature specification provided by a QA team and produce a structured test scope recommendation. You must reason carefully about:

1. What the change directly affects (functional scope).
2. What adjacent areas may break as a side-effect (smoke scope).
3. What existing functionality could regress due to this change (regression scope).
4. Which system integrations or data flows must be validated end-to-end (integration scope).
5. What non-obvious or edge-case behaviour is worth probing (exploratory scope).
6. How deep the coverage should be, justified by the change type and risk level.
7. A rough indicative test case count to help the team plan effort.
8. What information is missing from the specification that would materially change your recommendation — these are clarification flags that a QA lead should resolve before finalising the test plan.

Important guidelines:
- Feature specifications in enterprise QA environments are often sparse or ambiguous.   Reason from what is given, and surface gaps explicitly in clarification_flags.
- Coverage depth should be calibrated to change type:
    LOW    → patch fix, config value change, certificate rotation
    MEDIUM → enhancement, hardware rollout, access control change
    HIGH   → new feature, new integration, major version upgrade
- Effort estimates should reflect manual testing (not automated), realistic for a   small QA team.
- Be specific. Generic test descriptions (e.g., "test the feature") are not useful.   Name the specific behaviour, flow, or data condition to test.

You must always return a single valid JSON object. Do not include markdown fences, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.

JSON schema:
{
  "spec_id": "string",
  "functional_tests": ["test description"],
  "smoke_tests": ["test description"],
  "regression_tests": ["test description"],
  "integration_tests": ["test description"],
  "exploratory_tests": ["test description"],
  "coverage_depth": {
    "level": "LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH",
    "justification": "brief reason"
  },
  "effort_estimate": {
    "min_test_cases": 0,
    "max_test_cases": 0,
    "notes": "brief notes"
  },
  "clarification_flags": ["missing information that would affect testing"]
}
